# Model Selection

## Model Selection

+ Overall objective: the best future real-world performance
  + Which model family?
  + What features?
  + Which values of hyperparameters? 

+ External factors: resources, laws, ethics, etc.


## Model Confirmation

+ Confirm generalisation 
  + performance on unseen data

. . .   

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1))
_temp = ax.broken_barh([(0, 80)], (10, 9), facecolors='tab:blue')
_temp = ax.broken_barh([(80, 20)], (10, 9), facecolors='tab:orange')
_temp = ax.text(40, 14.5, 'Training Data (80%)', color='white', fontsize=12, ha='center', va='center')
_temp = ax.text(90, 14.5, 'Test (20%)', color='white', fontsize=12, ha='center', va='center')
_temp = ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
_temp = ax.set_ylim(5, 25)
_temp = ax.axis('off')
plt.show()
```   
+ Training / test split gives
  + a fitted model
  + a performance estimate

## The Learning Curve

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
train_sizes = np.linspace(10, 500, 100)
test_err = 0.5 - 0.2 * np.exp(-train_sizes / 100)

_temp = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
_temp = plt.plot(train_sizes, test_err, 'r-', lw=2, label='True Generalisation Accuracy')
_temp = plt.xlabel('Number of Training Instances')
_temp = plt.ylabel('Accuracy = 1 - Error')
_temp = plt.title('Theoretical Learning Curve')
_temp = plt.legend(loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## The Learning Curve and Estimates

+ For the learning curve, we assume an infinite test set
  + True performance

+ The more data is used to fit a (good) model, the better

+ If the model is trained on insufficient data, the generalisation estimate is too low
  + Pessimistic bias

## Training / Test Trade-off

+ A small test set means sensitivity to each instance
  + High variance of the performance estimate
  
+ Training / test split is a trade-off for performance estimate
  + Pessimistic bias vs high variance


## Model Selection and Testing

+ If we use the test set to choose a model, we will use the same set **repeatedly**
  + ...and we estimate the performance on the same set
  + An example of data leakage
    + The test set no longer provides a reliable estimate of future performance

+ The test set must not be used for model selection

## Training / Validation / Test

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2))
_temp = ax.broken_barh([(0, 60)], (10, 9), facecolors='tab:blue')
_temp = ax.broken_barh([(60, 20)], (10, 9), facecolors='tab:green')
_temp = ax.broken_barh([(80, 20)], (10, 9), facecolors='tab:orange')
_temp = ax.text(30, 14.5, 'Training (60%)', color='white', fontsize=12, ha='center', va='center')
_temp = ax.text(70, 14.5, 'Validation (20%)', color='white', fontsize=10, ha='center', va='center')
_temp = ax.text(90, 14.5, 'Test (20%)', color='white', fontsize=12, ha='center', va='center')
_temp = ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
_temp = ax.set_ylim(5, 25)
_temp = ax.axis('off')
plt.show()
```

+ The training set is for fitting the model
+ The validation is for selecting the model
  + model family, feature selection, tuning
+ The test set is for generalisation assessment

## The Unlucky Split Problem

+ Risks of a fixed training / validation split:
  + all the "easy" examples in validation (overly optimistic)
  + all the outliers in validation (overly pessimistic)

+ High variance in model selection 
+ Pessimistic performance bias 
  + The model overfits to the validation set and then fails on the test set

# Cross-Validation

## Cross-Validation Properties

+ Multiple splits instead of one fixed split
  + several iterations
+ Each instance may be used for training and for testing
  + but in different iterations
+ "Unlucky splits" are averaged out

## CV as Pipeline Assessment

+ Cross-validation does not estimate performance of any single model
+ Cross-validation assesses a "pipeline"
  + How to go from data to a fitted model
+ The best pipeline is trained on all training data and then tested on a hold-out set
  + After the training / test split, the training set is used for CV


## Leave-One-Out CV (LOOCV)

+ Train on all but one and test on that one
+ Repeat for each instance

\

+ Largest possible training set $\Rightarrow$ lowest bias
+ Smallest validation set $\Rightarrow$ high variance
  + and the training sets are correlated
+ Normally, computationally expensive 

## LOOCV for Linear Regression

+ In practice, LOOCV is used only for linear regression
  + and some derivated methods
+ For linear regressio, LOOCV can be calculated analytically using the fitted model
  + Computationally cheap
  + Does not add much (other than interpretation)

## Leave-p-Out CV

+ Train on all but $p$ instances and test on the rest
+ Repeat for all possible combinations of $p$ instances
+ Computationally intractable
  + exponential growth in $p$

## Monte-Carlo CV

+ Randomly select several instances for testing and the rest is used for training
  + Usually a fixed fraction is selected, 10% or 20%
+ Repeat $M$ times

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.5))
np.random.seed(42) # Keeps the random layout stable across slide renders

for i in range(4):
    # Create 100 total units, randomly pick 20 for validation (orange)
    indices = np.arange(100)
    val_indices = np.random.choice(indices, size=20, replace=False)
    
    # Map the indices to (start_pos, width) tuples required by broken_barh
    blue_ranges = [(x, 1) for x in indices if x not in val_indices]
    orange_ranges = [(x, 1) for x in val_indices]
    
    _temp = ax.broken_barh(blue_ranges, (10 - i*3, 2), facecolors='tab:blue', alpha=0.6)
    _temp = ax.broken_barh(orange_ranges, (10 - i*3, 2), facecolors='tab:orange', alpha=0.9)

_temp = ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
_temp = ax.set_ylim(-2, 13)
_temp = ax.axis('off')
plt.show()
```  

## $k$-Fold CV

+ Split data into $k$ non-overlapping blocks (folds) of equal size
+ Repeat $k$ times: use one block for validation and the remaining $k-1$ for training

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
for i in range(5):
    _temp = ax.broken_barh([(0, 100)], (12 - i*3, 2), facecolors='tab:blue', alpha=0.4)
    _temp = ax.broken_barh([(i*20, 20)], (12 - i*3, 2), facecolors='tab:orange', alpha=0.9)
    _temp = ax.text(i*20 + 10, 12 - i*3 + 1, 'Val', color='white', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
_temp = ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
_temp = ax.set_ylim(-2, 15)
_temp = ax.axis('off')
plt.title("5-Fold Cross Validation")
plt.show()

```

## Monte-Carlo vs $k$-Fold

+ Monte-Carlo decouples training set size and the number of repetitions 
  + Variance and bias are controlled independently
  
+ Monte-Carlo with $1/k$ testing and $k$-fold have the same bias

+ $k$-fold ensures non-overlapping test sets
  + lower variance
  + $2$-fold allows also non-overlapping training sets
    + statistical tests work

## Repeated k-Fold CV

+ Repeat $R$ times
  + Randomly re-shuffle the data
  + Perform $k$-fold CV
+ Averaging across $k \times R$ models
+ Often combines advantages of Monte-Carlo and $k$-fold

## Scikit-Learn Specifics

+ `KFold(n_splits=5)` in `scikit-learn` is deterministic by default!
  + To ensure it works for time series
  + Catastrophic if the data is sorted by target
+  `KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True)` reshuffles randomly

+ `RepeatedKFold` for regression and balanced classification

+ `RepeatedStratifiedKFold` for imbalanced classes
  + for a very small class, Monte-Carlo wins
  
## Cross-Validation Bottomline

+ CV solves the "unlucky split" issue

+ No issue for large datasets
  + Training / validation / test is fine for model selection
  
+ Model selection on smaller datasets:
  + Nested cross-validation to avoid data leakage
    + Model is selected on each train fold separately using CV

# The Limits of (Cross-)Validation

## Expected Performance

+ The performance on the test set is used to estimate the generalisation ability
  + Cross-validation reduces the variance of the estimate

+ Hidden assumption!  
  + Expected (=mean) performance exists
  
+ Not all distributions have a mean

## Heavy-Tail Distributions

+ Some processes produce extreme outliers
+ Example: Normal vs. Cauchy vs. Student $t$ 

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
x = np.linspace(-10, 10, 400)
_temp = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
_temp = plt.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x), 'b-', lw=2, label='Normal')
_temp = plt.plot(x, stats.cauchy.pdf(x), 'r-', lw=2, label='Cauchy')
_temp = plt.plot(x, stats.t.pdf(x, df=1), 'g--', lw=2, label='Student')
_temp = plt.xlim(-8, 8)
_temp = plt.title("Probability Density: Notice the fat tails of Cauchy")
_temp = plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```

## The Shooting Example

+ A blindfolded person shoots at a straight wall
+ The angle is chosen uniformly at random
+ The bullet's location on the wall follows a Student $t$-distribution with $1$ degree of freedom
+ The mean location of all bullet holes is mathematically undefined 

## CV Non-Convergence

+ If errors follow a heavy-tailed distribution, adding more CV folds or more data doesn't stabilize the mean error

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
np.random.seed(42)
cauchy_data = np.abs(np.random.standard_cauchy(1000))
norm_data = np.abs(np.random.standard_normal(1000))

run_mean_cauchy = np.cumsum(cauchy_data) / np.arange(1, 1001)
run_mean_norm = np.cumsum(norm_data) / np.arange(1, 1001)

_temp = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
_temp = plt.plot(run_mean_norm, 'b-', label='Gaussian Error (Converges)')
_temp = plt.plot(run_mean_cauchy, 'r-', label='Cauchy Error (Jumps unpredictably)')
_temp = plt.xlabel('Number of Folds/Evaluations')
_temp = plt.ylabel('Running Average of Error')
_temp = plt.title('Failure of the Law of Large Numbers')
_temp = plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```  

## Practical Heavy-Tailed Data 

+ Catastrophe insurance 
+ High-frequency trading: flash crashes
  + Nassim Taleb's black swans
+ Internet traffic / server load: virality
+ Epidemiology: super-spreader event

## Dealing with Heavy Tails

+ Replace the performance metric
  + Median instead mean
  + Log transformation
  
+ Do testing / (cross-)validaion as normal  

# Hyperparameter Tuning

## Grid Search with CV

+ Define a discrete grid of hyperparameter values
  + often in the log scale
+ Try every possible combination

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cal_X, cal_y = fetch_california_housing(return_X_y=True)
cal_X_sample, cal_y_sample = cal_X[:1000], cal_y[:1000] # Subsample for speed
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_sc = scaler.fit_transform(cal_X_sample)

grid = {'alpha': [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]}
gs = GridSearchCV(Ridge(), grid, cv=3)
_temp = gs.fit(X_sc, cal_y_sample)

df_gs = pd.DataFrame(gs.cv_results_)[['param_alpha', 'mean_test_score', 'rank_test_score']]
df_gs.columns = ['Ridge Alpha', 'Mean CV R²', 'Rank']
print(df_gs.to_markdown(index=False))

```

## Random Search

+ Sample hyperparameters randomly
  + Define suitable distributions
+ Repeat a fixed number of times

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
param_dist = {
    'alpha': stats.loguniform(1e-2, 1e1),
    'l1_ratio': stats.uniform(0, 1)
}
rs = RandomizedSearchCV(ElasticNet(), param_dist, n_iter=3, cv=3, random_state=42)
_temp = rs.fit(X_sc, cal_y_sample)

df_rs = pd.DataFrame(rs.cv_results_)[['param_alpha', 'param_l1_ratio', 'mean_test_score']]
df_rs['param_alpha'] = df_rs['param_alpha'].apply(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")
df_rs['param_l1_ratio'] = df_rs['param_l1_ratio'].apply(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")
df_rs.columns = ['EN Alpha', 'L1 Ratio', 'Mean CV R²']
print(df_rs.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Grid vs Random Search

* Random search covers more in many dimensions

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))

# Grid
xg = np.linspace(0, 1, 4)
yg = np.linspace(0, 1, 4)
Xg, Yg = np.meshgrid(xg, yg)
_temp = axes[0].scatter(Xg, Yg, color='blue')
_temp = axes[0].set_title('Grid Search (16 trials)\nOnly 4 unique values per axis')

# Random
np.random.seed(42)
xr = np.random.uniform(0, 1, 16)
yr = np.random.uniform(0, 1, 16)
_temp = axes[1].scatter(xr, yr, color='red')
_temp = axes[1].set_title('Random Search (16 trials)\n16 unique values per axis')

for ax in axes:
    _temp = ax.set_xticks([])
    _temp = ax.set_yticks([])
    _temp = ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 1.1)
    _temp = ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.1)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```

## Tuning as ML Task

+ Finding hyperparameters is itself an optimization problem!

+ We can use established ML models
  + Brute-force search
  + Heuristic search
  + Online bandits
  + Bayesian optimization
  
  
# Performance Metrics

## Accuracy Fail (Imbalanced Classes)

+ Accuracy = (Correct Predictions) / (Total Predictions)
+ $1$ in $1000$ is infected $\Rightarrow$ $99.9$% accuracy for free

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
y_true = np.array([0]*999 + [1]*1)
y_pred = np.array([0]*1000) # Always predict majority

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=['Normal', 'Infected'])
_temp = disp.plot(cmap='Blues', values_format='d')
plt.show()

```

## Alternatives to Accuracy

+ Precision: $\frac{\text{True Positive}}{\text{True Positive} + \text{False Positive}}$
  + Selection rate ("found to be infected")

+ Recall: $\frac{\text{True Positive}}{\text{True Positive} + \text{False Negative}}$
  + Detection rate ("infected to be found")

+ F1 score: harmonic mean of Precision and Recall

+ Mean recall

+ Matthews Correlation Coefficient


## MSE Fail (Outliers)

+ Mean Squared Error heavily penalizes large errors
+ One single mistake (outlier) can ruin the entire model fit

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 15)
y = 2 * x + 1 + np.random.normal(0, 1, 15)
y[13] = -15 # Extreme outlier

lr = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
hr = HuberRegressor().fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y) # Robust to outliers

_temp = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
_temp = plt.scatter(x, y, color='black', label='Data')
_temp = plt.plot(x, lr.predict(x.reshape(-1,1)), 'r-', lw=2, label='Fitted for MSE (Pulled down)')
_temp = plt.plot(x, hr.predict(x.reshape(-1,1)), 'g--', lw=2, label='Fitted for MAE/Robust (Ignores outlier)')
_temp = plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## MAE and MAPE

+ Mean Absolute Error: $\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N |y_i - \hat{y}_i|$
  + robust to outliers

+ Mean Absolute Percentage Error: $\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left|\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right|$
  + Business-friendly ("5% off on average")
  + Needs values away from $0$


## Metrics as a Managerial Decision

+ Metrics translate ML performance into business value
  + False negatives in medical lab cost lives
    + optimize recall
  + False positives in spam filter prevent communication
    + optimize precision
    
+ Domain experts dictate the metrics
  + Cost matrix / custom loss function
  + Instance weights

# Pre-Processing and Pipelines

## Pre-Processing

+ Raw data is rarely ready for algorithms

+ Common steps
  + Finding outliers
  + Handling missing values (imputation)
  + Re-encoding categorical variables
  + Scaling numerical variables


## Scaling-Invariant vs Not-Invariant

+ Scaling-invariance: scaling features does not change prediction

+ Scaling-invariant models:
  + ordinary linear regression
  + decision trees

+ Not scaling-invariant models:
  + Ridge / LASSO regression 
  + $k$-Nearest Neighbours 

## Scaling Strategies

+ Method-based
  + `StandardScaler`
  + `MinMaxScaler`
  + `RobustScaler`

+ Domain-based
  + Custom range (time, angle, marks, etc.)
  + Assumed distribution
  + `Normalizer`
  
## Scikit-Learn Scalers

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler, Normalizer

# Generate synthetic dataset
np.random.seed(42)
n_samples = 30
cov = [[2, 0], [0, 4]] 

X0 = np.random.multivariate_normal([10, 3], cov, n_samples)
X1 = np.random.multivariate_normal([10, 7], cov, n_samples)
X = np.vstack((X0, X1))
y = np.hstack((np.zeros(n_samples), np.ones(n_samples)))

# Set up a 2x3 grid where the original data spans the entire left column
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3, width_ratios=[1.2, 1, 1])

ax_orig = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0])
ax_std = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
ax_min = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
ax_rob = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])
ax_norm = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])

def plot_scaled(ax, X_scaled, title, show_axes=True, limits=None):
    _temp = ax.scatter(X_scaled[y==0, 0], X_scaled[y==0, 1], s=8, alpha=0.6, c='blue', label='Mean (10, 3)')
    _temp = ax.scatter(X_scaled[y==1, 0], X_scaled[y==1, 1], s=8, alpha=0.6, c='red', label='Mean (10, 7)')
    _temp = ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    
    if show_axes:
        _temp = ax.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5, zorder=0)
        _temp = ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5, zorder=0)
        
    _temp = ax.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.7)
    
    if limits:
        _temp = ax.set_xlim(limits)
        _temp = ax.set_ylim(limits)
        _temp = ax.set_aspect('equal', adjustable='box')
    else:
        _temp = ax.set_aspect('equal', 'datalim')

# Plot Original and Scaled Versions
plot_scaled(ax_orig, X, "Original Data")

shared_limits = (-2.2, 2.2)
plot_scaled(ax_std, StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), "StandardScaler\n(Mean=0, Var=1)", limits=shared_limits)
plot_scaled(ax_min, MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(X), "MinMaxScaler\n(Range [0, 1])", limits=shared_limits)
plot_scaled(ax_rob, RobustScaler().fit_transform(X), "RobustScaler\n(Resistant to Outliers)", limits=shared_limits)
plot_scaled(ax_norm, Normalizer().fit_transform(X), "Normalizer\n(Maps to Unit Circle)", limits=shared_limits)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```  

## Pre-Processing and Splits

+ Pre-preprocessing is determined by training data
  + For example, the scaling transformation

+ The same procedure is applied to all data points 

+ Common mistakes:
  + `StandardScaler` separately for each subset
    + Fails on one-element test set
  + `StandardScaler` before split
    + Data leakage!

## StandardScaler Data Leakage

+ A sample from normal distribution

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# Simulating leakage
np.random.seed(42)
X_full = np.random.normal(100, 25, 100).reshape(-1, 1)

# Bad Way
scaler_bad = StandardScaler().fit(X_full)
X_scaled_bad = scaler_bad.transform(X_full)
X_tr_bad, X_te_bad = train_test_split(X_scaled_bad, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# Good Way
X_tr_raw, X_te_raw = train_test_split(X_full, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
scaler_good = StandardScaler().fit(X_tr_raw)
X_tr_good = scaler_good.transform(X_tr_raw)
X_te_good = scaler_good.transform(X_te_raw)

df_leak = pd.DataFrame({
    "Method": ["Scaled Before Split (Leakage)", "Scaled After Split (Correct)"],
    "Train Mean": [f"{X_tr_bad.mean():.4f}", f"{X_tr_good.mean():.4f}"],
    "Test Mean": [f"{X_te_bad.mean():.4f}", f"{X_te_good.mean():.4f}"]
})
print(df_leak.to_markdown(index=False))
```


## Pipelines in Scikit-Learn I

+ For cross-validation, we need to define pre-processing for each training part
  + Error-prone if manual

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('classifier', Ridge())])
pipe_nonames = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge())
```

+ Pipelines automate the correct sequence 
  + The scaler will not see the validation fold

## Pipelines in Scikit-Learn II

+ A pipeline can include any number of steps
  + For example, imputation, feature engineering, scaling, prediction
  
+ `Pipeline.fit()` calls
  + `.fit()` followed by `.transform()` for each step except the last one
  + `.fit()` on the last step

# Model Development and Deployment

## The ML Life Cycle in Industry

1. Business problem and KPIs
2. Data collection and fundamental pre-processing
3. Model selection and assessment
4. Validation and governance
5. Deployment, monitoring and maintenance

## Baseline

+ A baseline method allows us to calibrate performance expectations
  + Data properties vs method properties
  
+ Baseline depends on the "state of the art"  
  + Predict the mean / most frequent class
  + $3$-NN or linear regression
  + The current method

## Development Tracking

+ Model development requires a lot of experimentation

+ Tracking helps
  + avoid data leakage
  + maintain consistency
  + justify decision
  + facilitate handovers
  
+ Tools such as MLflow log models, parameters and scores


## Model Governance

+ Pre-deployment checks
  + Final validation scores
    + Ideally, the test data are not available to the developers
  + Security checks
  + Stability and performance checks

+ Compliance
  + GDPR, EDI, etc.

+ Traceability and monitoring

## Pre-Deployment Assessment

+ Shadow deployment
  + The new model makes predictions on live data in the background, but the outside world sees only the old model

+ A/B testing
  + Small proportion of the real work is done by the new model
  + Business KPIs are compared between the old and new models

## Model Monitoring

+ Models degrade over time

+ Data drift
  + The distribution of instances is different

+ Concept drift
  + The dependence between target and instance is different
